concepts.name: Composition and Mandate of the Cabinet Mission (1946)
key_dimensions: Three members: Pethick-Lawrence (Secretary of State), Stafford Cripps (Board of Trade), A.V. Alexander (Admiralty) — UPSC trap: confusing roles/portfolios
Distinction from earlier missions (Cripps Mission 1942) — what changed in British intent
Mandate: To discuss transfer of power and set up machinery for framing a constitution, NOT to partition India
Why Wavell (Viceroy) was present but not a 'member' of the Mission — a common confusion point

concepts.name: Rejection of Pakistan Demand and the Two-Nation Theory
key_dimensions: Cabinet Mission explicitly rejected a fully sovereign Pakistan — reasons stated (minority Muslims in Pakistan, economic unviability, defense issues)
Distinction between Cabinet Mission's rejection and Congress's acceptance of partition later in June 1947
Muslim League's paradoxical acceptance of the plan despite rejection of Pakistan — strategic motivation
How the Mission tried to address League's concerns through grouping scheme as an alternative to partition

concepts.name: Three-Tier Federal Structure Proposed by Cabinet Mission
key_dimensions: Three tiers: Union (Centre), Groups of Provinces, Individual Provinces — UPSC trap: order and jurisdiction of each tier
Union subjects limited to only three: Foreign Affairs, Defence, and Communications (plus finance for these) — 'only' clause trap
Residuary powers with Provinces, not the Union — contrast with actual Constitution of India
Groups could have their own executives, legislatures, and constitutions — semi-autonomous nature

concepts.name: Grouping of Provinces: Sections A, B, and C
key_dimensions: Section A: Madras, Bombay, UP, Bihar, CP, Orissa (Hindu-majority, Congress stronghold)
Section B: Punjab, NWFP, Sind, Baluchistan (Muslim-majority, northwest)
Section C: Bengal and Assam — UPSC trap: Assam's inclusion in Section C despite Congress objection
Compulsory vs. optional grouping — the central controversy between Congress and League interpretations
Congress objection: NWFP and Assam should not be compulsorily grouped; League insisted on compulsory grouping

concepts.name: Constituent Assembly: Composition and Election Method
key_dimensions: Total seats: 389 — 292 from British India provinces, 93 from Princely States, 4 from Chief Commissioners' Provinces
Indirect election: Provincial assemblies elected CA members (not direct election) — method of proportional representation by single transferable vote
Communal breakdown: General (Hindu), Muslim, Sikh seats in proportion to population
Princely states' representatives to be nominated, not elected — a democratic inconsistency noted by critics

concepts.name: Congress Acceptance of Cabinet Mission Plan: Conditions and Interpretations
key_dimensions: Congress accepted the long-term plan (Constituent Assembly) but with its own interpretation of grouping being optional
Nehru's July 1946 statement that Congress was 'free to change or modify the Cabinet Mission Plan' — triggered League's withdrawal
Distinction between Congress accepting the plan 'as a whole' vs. accepting specific clauses — trap for MCQs
Congress rejection of the Interim Government proposal initially — why and when they reversed

concepts.name: Muslim League's Acceptance and Subsequent Withdrawal
key_dimensions: League accepted the plan on June 6, 1946 — rare instance of League accepting a Congress-included framework
Jinnah's strategic calculation: grouping scheme as a stepping stone to Pakistan
Withdrawal triggered by Nehru's July 1946 press conference statement — sequence of events is a UPSC trap
League's call for 'Direct Action Day' (August 16, 1946) after withdrawal — consequences (Great Calcutta Killings)

concepts.name: Interim Government Formation (September 1946)
key_dimensions: Nehru as Vice-President of Executive Council (not Prime Minister) — title distinction is a UPSC trap
Congress initially formed the government without League; League joined later in October 1946 — two-phase formation
Liaquat Ali Khan as Finance Member — used position to obstruct Congress policies (People's Budget controversy)
Functioning as a de facto Cabinet despite technically being Executive Council of Viceroy — constitutional ambiguity

concepts.name: Constituent Assembly Sessions and League's Non-Participation
key_dimensions: CA first met on December 9, 1946 — Muslim League boycotted; Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha was temporary chairman
Dr. Rajendra Prasad elected permanent Chairman — UPSC trap: confusing with Ambedkar's role as Drafting Committee Chairman
Objectives Resolution moved by Nehru on December 13, 1946
League's non-participation rendered the CA unrepresentative — used by British as reason to reconsider the plan

concepts.name: The Grouping Dispute: Legal vs. Political Interpretation
key_dimensions: Cabinet Mission's own clarification (May 25, 1946) that grouping was compulsory at initial stage — Congress still disagreed
Federal Court (India) was never approached for legal arbitration — political resolution was attempted instead
Lord Wavell's role in trying to mediate the grouping interpretation dispute
This dispute as the fundamental reason why the Cabinet Mission Plan ultimately failed to be implemented

concepts.name: Princely States and Cabinet Mission Plan
key_dimensions: Paramountcy cannot be transferred to the new Dominion — States technically free to negotiate their own terms
Cabinet Mission's statement on lapse of paramountcy — implications for integration of princely states
No provision for compulsory accession of princely states — contrast with Sardar Patel's later integration policy
How this ambiguity contributed to problems with Hyderabad, Kashmir, and Junagadh later

concepts.name: Cabinet Mission Plan vs. Cripps Mission (1942): Key Differences
key_dimensions: Cripps 1942: offered Dominion Status post-war + right to secede; Cabinet Mission 1946: no right to secede, no full Pakistan
Cripps offered province-wise option to stay out of Union; Cabinet Mission offered grouping as alternative
Both missions rejected by both Congress and League — but for different reasons in each case
Change in British strategic interest: 1942 (war necessity) vs. 1946 (genuine withdrawal planning)

concepts.name: Role of Stafford Cripps in Cabinet Mission Negotiations
key_dimensions: Cripps was the primary negotiator and had prior India experience (1942 Mission)
His personal sympathy with Congress — perceived bias by Muslim League
Cripps-Azad correspondence controversy — alleged informal assurances given to Congress about grouping
His role in drafting the technical details of the three-tier structure

concepts.name: Short-Term Plan: Interim Government Proposal of Cabinet Mission
key_dimensions: Distinction between long-term plan (Constituent Assembly) and short-term plan (Interim Government) — often confused
Original proposal: Coalition Interim Government with 6 Congress + 5 League + 3 minorities
Congress objected to parity with League and to League nominating a non-League Muslim
Eventually Nehru-led government formed without League's initial participation — sequence matters for exam

concepts.name: Cabinet Mission Plan and the Question of Minorities
key_dimensions: Sikhs not given a separate group despite demands — no Section for Punjab Sikhs alone
Scheduled Castes representation: included under 'General' category, not separate communal category — Ambedkar's objection
Christians, Anglo-Indians, and other minorities: token representation in Constituent Assembly
Cabinet Mission's refusal to create more religious categories — contrast with Communal Award (1932)

concepts.name: Why the Cabinet Mission Plan Failed: Multi-Causal Analysis
key_dimensions: Interpretational conflict over compulsory grouping — Congress vs. League vs. Mission's own clarification
Nehru's July 1946 statement as immediate trigger for League's withdrawal
British inability to enforce the plan — lack of political will post-WWII exhaustion
Attlee's February 1947 announcement (deadline for withdrawal by June 1948) effectively superseded the plan, leading to Mountbatten Plan

concepts.name: Cabinet Mission Plan and Gandhi's Position
key_dimensions: Gandhi initially opposed: called the plan a 'post-dated cheque' (echoing his 1942 criticism of Cripps) — but later nuanced
Gandhi's role in convincing Congress Working Committee to accept the plan
His opposition to Nehru becoming Congress President (July 1946) — feared Nehru's statement would derail negotiations
Gandhi's 'one-man boundary force' approach vs. political negotiations — tension between moral and political strategies

concepts.name: Transition from Cabinet Mission Plan to Mountbatten Plan (1947)
key_dimensions: Atlee's statement of February 20, 1947 announcing Mountbatten as new Viceroy and June 1948 deadline — bypassed Cabinet Mission framework
How League's Direct Action and communal violence made the Cabinet Mission's unified India framework untenable
Mountbatten Plan (June 3, 1947) accepted partition — the 'last resort' after Cabinet Mission failure
Cabinet Mission Plan's legacy: many of its federal ideas influenced actual Constitution (e.g., Constituent Assembly process, though three-tier structure was abandoned)

concepts.name: Wavell Plan vs. Cabinet Mission Plan: Overlapping Timelines
key_dimensions: Wavell Plan (Simla Conference, 1945): precursor attempt to form Executive Council — failed due to Jinnah's veto on Muslim nominees
Key difference: Wavell Plan did not address constitution-making; Cabinet Mission did — scope distinction
Both failed due to Congress-League disagreement on Muslim representation — common thread
Wavell replaced by Mountbatten in March 1947 — why, and how it changed British India policy direction
